### Revision 2 — One persistent shell-drawn bottom bar is the taskbar and holds the maximized window's controls; sized windows carry bottom tags, not a title band

`superseded` · `@legeos.decision.one-persistent-bottom-bar-tags-not-bands/2` · scope `path "compositor/lege-comp/**"`, `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "interfaces/wayland/**"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"` · topic `bottom-bar`

A single shell-drawn bottom bar is always visible, over application windows and on Home, and reserves an Edge::Bottom exclusive zone. It is the output's full width: Home chip at the left (a pointer route to the Home Field, so a bare Super tap is not the only one), then the taskbar, then the machine cluster at the right end. Taskbar: LegeOS window groups first (one entry each in the group accent), then one entry per open application (a single-window application is that window), parked windows included and dimmed — Home places no tile for a running or parked window, so the bar is the only place one exists, and a click on a parked entry unshelves it before activating it. Hovering an entry after a dwell opens a second row above the bar listing its windows, a grace period closes it, a click activates. Machine cluster, right to left: an account chip, the clock, the network indicator and one readings chip (charge, and Muted when the machine is muted). The account chip opens a popover inside the bar surface holding Settings, the volume and brightness controls and the session actions (lock, suspend, log out, restart, shut down; the three that end the session take a second click), which is the only pointer route to them now that Home carries no Session or Settings widget. Bottom-right of all of it: park, maximize and close for the activated window when it is maximized. The compositor-drawn title band above every window is retired: a non-maximized window carries compositor-drawn tags on its bottom edge, a name tag bottom-left (title, group accent stripe; the grab-to-move and group-drop affordance) and contiguous control tags bottom-right; a maximized window on an output with a bottom exclusive zone draws no tags, and draws them again whenever no such zone is claimed, so controls never vanish when the shell is dead. The corner resize grip is removed; resize is the margin ring outside every edge and corner. A fullscreen window fills the whole output — Output::logical, over the bar's zone — and the compositor stacks it above the bar (WindowService::stacking_order's one exception to the fixed layer order: above ShellOverlay and Notification, never above SystemModal, Recovery or SecureLock); the bar surface stays mapped and keeps its zone, and a dwell on the output's bottom edge suspends the exception so the bar is drawn over the fullscreen window for as long as the pointer stays on the reserved strip. None of this is configurable.

**Context.** The user's hands-on runs showed a disconnect between Home and open windows: a mouse-only user had no persistent route between windows because Home is momentary and Alt+Tab is keyboard, and a window's controls sat at the top while the user's attention and the proposed taskbar sit at the bottom. The user first proposed moving the band to the bottom with a Windows 3.1 style window-list box, then replaced that with the shared bar: 'every open window shares the bar and the bar does double duty as a taskbar'. The hover-row behaviour is ported from cosmic-app-list (GPL-3, libcosmic); behaviour only, no code copied into this AGPL-3 repository. The 2026-09-08 run added the rest: docs/garden/garden.md's division of labour — Home deals with your things, the bar deals with the machine — made the scattered Session/Settings/sound/battery widgets one cluster; 'full screen mode should be genuinely full screen with taskbar mouseover' and 'doing away with the Super button as only way to get to home screen' are the fullscreen, peek and Home-chip clauses.

**Consequences.** Supersedes the clause of @legeos.decision.home-is-momentary-and-placeable-objects-are-containers that Home panels 'reserve no work area while an application is visible'; the rest of that decision (momentary Home, placeable containers, no loose files) stands. @legeos.work.home-panel-and-dock-layouts' check home-only-no-exclusive-zone is historical. Output::usable's refusal of a zone that leaves less than 96x32 remains the safety clause. compositor/COMPOSITOR.md's band sections are rewritten for tags, and its set_fullscreen row and its Home-visibility section carry the stacking exception and the peek. The exclusive zone is a floor on the surface's thickness so the hover row and the account popover can grow the bar surface without reflowing windows (prose-only change to lege-shell-v1.xml). Two earlier behaviours are retired: the bar no longer shrinks to its chips (a right-aligned cluster on a left-anchored surface is at the right of nothing), and the shell no longer destroys its own bar while a window is fullscreen (that released the zone and reflowed every maximized window on the output, twice). WindowRecord gains a fullscreen_restore slot of its own so maximize-then-fullscreen restores both; on_outputs_changed re-derives a fullscreen window's geometry and never repairs it, because is_recoverable measures a tag strip against usable() and a fullscreen window has no strip.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.one-persistent-bottom-bar-tags-not-bands/1` · **superseded by** `@legeos.decision.one-persistent-bottom-bar-tags-not-bands/3`

The user first proposed moving the band to the bottom with a Windows 3.1 style window-list box, then replaced that with the shared bar: 'every open window shares the bar and the bar does double duty as a taskbar'. The hover-row behaviour is ported from cosmic-app-list (GPL-3, libcosmic); behaviour only, no code copied into this AGPL-3 repository.

**Consequences.** Supersedes the clause of @legeos.decision.home-is-momentary-and-placeable-objects-are-containers that Home panels 'reserve no work area while an application is visible'; the rest of that decision (momentary Home, placeable containers, no loose files) stands. @legeos.work.home-panel-and-dock-layouts' check home-only-no-exclusive-zone is historical. Output::usable's refusal of a zone that leaves less than 96x32 remains the safety clause. compositor/COMPOSITOR.md's band sections are rewritten for tags. The exclusive zone is a floor on the surface's thickness so the hover row can grow the bar surface without reflowing windows (prose-only change to lege-shell-v1.xml).

**superseded by** `@legeos.decision.one-persistent-bottom-bar-tags-not-bands/2`

## legeos.decision.one-privileged-host-daemon

### Revision 2 — D4/ADR-0003 — One privileged host daemon (lege-hostd): updates, deployments, driver authority, storage reserve, hardware profile; timezone policy stays in sessiond

`active` · `@legeos.decision.one-privileged-host-daemon/2` · scope `path "distro/policy/dbus/**"`, `path "distro/policy/polkit/**"`, `path "services/templar-hostd/**"`

lege-hostd (system bus org.legeos.Host, one polkit policy org.legeos.host.*, AppArmor profile) hosts Updates, Deployments (BootManager trait), Drivers/GPU mode, Storage reserve and Hardware profile. It keeps an on-disk transaction journal and runs apt as a child transient unit. Timezone/location policy is NOT in hostd: it is network-facing and lives in lege-sessiond, setting the zone via polkit-gated org.freedesktop.timedate1.

**Context.** The docs' updated, 'one driver authority', storage reserve and locationd are all root policy over apt/systemd; each as its own root daemon multiplies privileged surfaces; untrusted geolocation JSON must not be parsed as root.

**Consequences.** Fewer privileged surfaces; one place for lege update, doctor support-violation checks and the hardware profile.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.one-privileged-host-daemon/1`

## legeos.decision.one-session-policy-daemon

### Revision 2 — D2/ADR-0001 — One user session policy daemon (lege-sessiond) hosting appd, associationd, providers, history, notifications, settings, projects, power, location as library crates

`active` · `@legeos.decision.one-session-policy-daemon/2` · scope `path "crates/templar-appd/**"`, `path "crates/templar-associationd/**"`, `path "crates/templar-session-core/**"`, `path "crates/templar-state/**"`, `path "services/templar-sessiond/**"`

lege-sessiond is the single user policy daemon (bus name org.legeos.Session). Application identity + launching (appd), the association broker (associationd), provider/autostart arbitration, history, notifications (org.freedesktop.Notifications when selected), typed settings, project sessions, power and timezone/location policy are separate library crates wired by a thin daemon over one SQLite state store (lege-state). Interfaces are domain-scoped and versioned (org.legeos.AppIdentity1, org.legeos.Associations1, ...) at separate object paths so a later split only relocates a bus name. Type=notify, Restart=on-failure, WatchdogSec; instances persisted and re-derived from systemd unit patterns after restart; history writes are non-fatal.

**Context.** The planning docs propose several services and note associationd 'probably as part of appd'; the user's Lubuntu install suffers from many daemons/applets with private state and no shared identity key; cross-daemon D-Bus adds the launch-registration and governor-blocking races the docs flag.

**Consequences.** One crash/restart unit and one place to explain decisions; cross-domain updates are transactions. filed and resourced remain separate processes. Crate boundaries keep the split reversible.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.one-session-policy-daemon/1`

## legeos.decision.pcmanfm-qt-is-the-file-manager

### Revision 2 — pcmanfm-qt is the session's file manager; lege-files leaves the composition

`active` · `@legeos.decision.pcmanfm-qt-is-the-file-manager/2` · scope `path "apps/templar-files/**"`, `path "crates/templar-session-core/src/providers.rs"`, `path "distro/app-manifests/**"`, `path "distro/seeds/selection.toml"`, `path "docs/architecture/files.md"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/src/surface/app.rs"`

The `file-manager` provider role and the desktop composition default to `pcmanfm-qt` (libfm-qt, Qt 6). `lege-files` stays a workspace member and a buildable `.deb` — it is the one real UI exercising `Browse1`, `Operations1`, `Previews1` and `Actions1` — but leaves `distro/seeds/selection.toml`, `legeos-desktop`, and the curated app manifests. `ProviderRole::FileManager` is derived from `Categories=FileManager` at priority 100 for the executable `pcmanfm-qt` and 50 otherwise, exactly as `Terminal` is derived from `TerminalEmulator` with kitty at 100; no shell code names an application any more. pcmanfm-qt must never be started with `--desktop`: Home is the desktop.

**Context.** The user, on the installed session, verbatim: "i want to integrate pcman, not use the Files app. pcman can talk to Filed where at all possible. Files is too rudimentary to be used for now." `legeos.work.standalone-file-manager/3` built `lege-files` and completed; what it produced is a working service client, not a file manager somebody can live in. Shipping a rudimentary one as the session default is a worse answer than shipping a complete third-party one and integrating it.

**Consequences.** Integration is limited to what libfm-qt offers from outside — there is no plugin API. Three routes exist and are taken: DES-EMA custom actions in `/usr/share/file-manager/actions/` shipped by `legeos-cli` ("Add to Home" over `HomeField1.PlaceFolder`, "Create project here" over `Projects1.Create`); a one-way bookmarks export from filed to `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/gtk-3.0/bookmarks`, the file libfm-qt's Places sidebar reads, with filed the authority and no import; and Trash, which needs nothing — filed's `Trash1` already implements the freedesktop Trash specification on the same directories libfm-qt uses. Two routes do not exist and are recorded as such: pcmanfm-qt's recents (`recently-used.xbel`) are not read by `Files.Recents1`, and pcmanfm-qt's Find cannot ask `Files.Search1`. Qt 6 selects the Wayland platform plugin on its own from `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` with `qt6-wayland` installed, so the session sets no `QT_QPA_PLATFORM`; the compositor forces server-side xdg-decoration, so a pcmanfm-qt window wears LegeOS chrome.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.pcmanfm-qt-is-the-file-manager/1`

## legeos.decision.perimeter-resize-selects-two-axes-by-side-half

### Revision 2 — Perimeter resize selects one horizontal and one vertical edge from the contacted side half

`active` · `@legeos.decision.perimeter-resize-selects-two-axes-by-side-half/2` · scope `path "compositor/templar-comp/**"`, `path "crates/templar-window/**"` · topic `window-perimeter-resize`

Compositor-owned pointer resize uses the eight-logical-pixel exterior perimeter. Pressing either half of any side selects the adjacent corner's horizontal and vertical edge, with exact midpoints assigned to right or bottom. The selected pair and origin geometry latch at press; motion resizes from that origin, anchors the opposite edges, applies the existing minimum size, and never inverts the rectangle. Hover and the active gesture show the matching diagonal cursor, including on DRM, then restore client cursor ownership. Client-requested xdg resize edges retain their protocol meaning and bypass side-half reinterpretation.

**Context.** The current implementation already removed the visible corner grip and owns an outside resize margin, but middle portions of a side still select one axis and DRM maps every named cursor to the arrow.

**Consequences.** Remove RESIZE_CORNER only after its selection role is replaced. Preserve bottom tags, stacking precedence, maximized/fullscreen exclusions, keyboard/recovery paths and current size minima. Defer dead zones and motion-selected secondary edges until the fixed mapping is evaluated. As implemented: the halves are measured from the frame's own origin (frame.y + frame.height / 2, and the same on x), so a window at a negative coordinate splits at its own middle rather than at zero. RESIZE_CORNER is deleted; it had no consumer outside geometry.rs. The edges-to-cursor mapping is ResizeEdges::cursor, a method returning the cursor-spec name rather than a typed icon, because lege-window must stay free of cursor-icon (xtask deps-check) and the compositor parses the name back at the boundary. Single-axis resize remains reachable exactly where the protocol asks for it: xdg_toplevel.resize and the XWayland equivalent do not route through resize_edges_at. The DRM half of the cursor requirement is written but has never been seen on screen; that observation needs a logout and is a user gate.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.perimeter-resize-selects-two-axes-by-side-half/1`

## legeos.decision.representation-ladder-is-the-organizing-principle

### Revision 1 — One object, one canonical route, many sizes of representation — the ladder organizes the whole shell

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.representation-ladder-is-the-organizing-principle/1` · scope `path "apps/templar-files/**"`, `path "crates/templar-field/**"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/**"` · topic `shell-design-language`

The representation ladder (Micro → Small → Wide → Large → Full) is the organizing principle of the LegeOS interface, governed by three rules. One object, one canonical route, many sizes of representation: a semantic object is never simultaneously represented by proxies of itself (no Projects drawer beside project tiles, no auto App tile beside a session tile, no launcher tile beside the search field), and enlarging an object yields a bigger surface of the same object with location, selection and navigation state preserved — never a different UI. Minimize useless space, not empty space: permanent chrome, permanent destination tiles and duplicate search fields are useless space to be recovered; a margin of empty field is a drop/throw target and stays. Objects reveal capability as physical area becomes available: representation selection considers shape (cols, rows), not just cell count; Micro/Small representations are information-first with manipulation revealed on hover/focus, Wide and above carry a conventional heading. Visually, LegeOS uses calm rectangular instruments: neutral substrate, restrained boundaries, typography-led hierarchy, with accent colour communicating state rather than application branding, rich texture living inside objects, and expansion spatially continuous — a tile grows from its place and collapses back into it.

**Context.** An external design review (2026-09-01) found the Home Field model substantially better than the visible interface and prescribed subtraction and consolidation rather than a new home-screen concept. Exploration verified its factual claims: eight default drawer tiles, a triple-nested expanded-drawer chrome (field breadcrumb → HomeSurfaceScreen rail+search → FileBrowserScreen sidebar+toolbar), cell-count-only representation selection, an unconditional 34px grab band, duplicated app/session tiles, and two search fields.

**Consequences.** The default Home reduces to Work (projects, sessions, trays), one adaptive Files object, and a minimal set of system surfaces; the application catalogue lives behind the omnibox. HomeSurfaceScreen and the launcher tile are retired. Every expandable surface gets a persistent state model consumed by all rungs. Existing saved layouts migrate through add-only merge-time rewrites, never a version refusal.

## legeos.decision.resourced-separate-process

### Revision 2 — D3/ADR-0002 — The resource governor (lege-resourced) is a separate, tiny, protected process that needs no D-Bus for emergency actions

`active` · `@legeos.decision.resourced-separate-process/2` · scope `path "crates/templar-types/src/unit.rs"`, `path "services/templar-resourced/**"`

lege-resourced runs as its own user process (org.legeos.Resources) with mlockall, MemoryLow, OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, high CPU/IO weight and no SQLite. Launch units are self-describing (app-legeos-<AppId>@<InstanceId>.service) so cgroup->instance identity is derived from /sys/fs/cgroup alone; foreground/visibility arrive as compositor signals; sessiond only enriches. Policy is a pure engine separated from cgroup writes and runs observe-only until recorded traces show sensible choices; then cache trim, throttling (memory.high + reclaim), checkpoint requests and whole-cgroup termination are enabled in stages.

**Context.** The governor must keep ticking under exactly the conditions that stall a daemon doing SQLite/fsync/D-Bus/desktop-file imports (full disk in the storage-reserve case, a panic in an unrelated domain).

**Consequences.** Two user daemons for policy instead of one; the governor is testable in isolation and survives sessiond restarts; lege doctor verifies its protection values.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.resourced-separate-process/1`

## legeos.decision.session-greeter-lock

### Revision 2 — D10/ADR-0010 — systemd-managed session (legeos-session.target), sessiond-arbitrated autostart, greetd + lege-greeter, compositor-owned lock screen

`active` · `@legeos.decision.session-greeter-lock/2` · scope `path "session/**"`

The session is legeos-session.target plus user units with explicit protection values, started by the lege-session entry from wayland-sessions/legeos.desktop; xdg-desktop-autostart.target is masked and lege-sessiond launches approved autostart entries with identity and cgroups (one provider per exclusive role). Greeter: greetd + lege-greeter, our own, speaking greetd's JSON IPC over its socket so that greetd owns PAM and the greeter links no authentication code. Lock screen: compositor-core ext-session-lock-v1.

**Context.** A full distribution needs a display manager and a session manager; the docs demand permissioned autostart and one provider per role. Revision 1 chose the cosmic-greeter fork on the reasoning that reusing the compositor avoids a second toolkit stack. ADR-0012 removed the compositor fork, which removed that reasoning with it: cosmic-greeter would have dragged libcosmic back into the dependency graph for the login screen alone, and the way to avoid a second toolkit stack is now for the greeter to use the same toolkit as the shell.

**Consequences.** One session stack; lege doctor checks the units and their protection values, and now also that every unit's ExecStart binary is actually installed. The greeter is ours to maintain, but it links no PAM, no shadow and nothing setuid — authentication stays entirely inside greetd.

**supersedes** `@legeos.decision.session-greeter-lock/1`

`superseded` · `@legeos.decision.session-greeter-lock/1` · scope `path "session/**"`

Greeter: greetd + the cosmic-greeter fork (reuses the compositor). Lock screen: compositor-core ext-session-lock-v1.

**Context.** A full distribution needs a display manager and a session manager; reusing the compositor for the greeter avoids a second toolkit stack; the docs demand permissioned autostart and one provider per role.

**Consequences.** One session stack; lege doctor checks the units and their protection values.

**superseded by** `@legeos.decision.session-greeter-lock/2`

## legeos.decision.task-system-four-scales-one-model

### Revision 1 — Window management has four scales over one task model: Home is a place, the island shows what runs, Taskfield is a compositor view of every window, the launcher starts; Alt+Tab walks every open window, Peek is the pointer's way out of fullscreen

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.task-system-four-scales-one-model/1` · scope `path "compositor/templar-comp/**"`, `path "crates/templar-types/src/action.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-window/**"`, `path "interfaces/wayland/**"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/**"` · topic `task-system`

Four scales, each answering one question and none duplicating another. HomeGarden asks what am I working on (a persistent place; it shows counts of running windows, never live previews, and never lists windows). The Task Island (the bar) asks what is running: one chip per task unit (an explicit group, or an application with its loose windows), never a title on the bar, a count for more than one window, a fan of at most four preview cards on dwell, and a hand-over to Taskfield above four; chip order is first-seen and never reorders on activation. A chip is the application's icon (a group wears its most recently activated member's), the name is a hover tooltip, and an initial is only the fallback when no icon resolves. Taskfield asks where are all my windows: a presentation mode of the compositor itself, entered by Super+Tab, the bottom-left corner dwell (Peek), the island's overflow, the launcher's arrow, or a place's 'N windows active' line. It is a VIEW, not a place: the compositor draws every client surface scaled at a presentation rectangle without sending a configure, laid out per output into sections by task unit (explicit groups first) with equal cards that never exceed the window's real size; selection highlights, it never moves geometry; the layout exists only while the mode is up and nothing about it is ever stored. The launcher (the Apps bar on bare Home) asks what can I start; Super+Space reveals Home with it focused. Alt+Tab walks every open application window (WindowService::alt_tab_order: mapped, parked ones included), most recently activated first, across every unit and output, frozen at the first press; Tab moves the HUD's selection and releasing the modifier activates it (unparking a parked window), while Escape, a click or another chord cancels; a window that closes or unmaps mid-walk leaves the list. Alt+` is the same walk within the current unit (the group when grouped, the application otherwise), parked members included. One model: templar_window::task::units, a pure function over the shell toplevels both the compositor and the shell hold, is the only grouping and ordering of windows; activation recency (mru_rank) is the only recency. One presentation state: WindowService::Presentation {Normal, HomeReveal, Taskfield}; a fullscreen window covers passive chrome only while Normal, and explicit navigation yields to nothing. Under a screen-filling window the bottom-left corner carries a two-pixel affordance; a dwell there is Peek (the island rises), a second dwell or motion past the island is Taskfield. Home's corner dwell moves to the top-left. Shell death inside Taskfield changes the labels, not the mode.

**Context.** Extrapolated from the external review 'TemplarOS does need a taskbar, but the taskbar should not be responsible for making every window discoverable' and the reviewer's follow-up drawing the line HomeGarden is a place, Taskfield is a view (source task-system-taskfield-island-peek-20260909). The reviewer's warning: if Taskfield positions acquire permanent meaning it becomes Desktop 2. Scoped on 2026-09-09 by three lanes against the tree at 01445f5: 852fb55 had already landed activation recency and the MRU switcher, the bar already had its Hint/Revealed presences with an edge dwell under fullscreen, and Smithay already renders a surface tree at any origin and scale in the screencopy path, so the doc's weighted packer, zoom ladder, frozen-generation machinery, TaskModel struct, and preview re-send on shell reconnect (screencopy is client-pull; the compositor holds no pixels) were not built. The user chose: full scope, Peek at the bottom-left corner displacing the Home corner, the volume and brightness sliders in the account popover, a -60 dB volume cutoff and a 10% backlight floor. Revised 2026-10-04 on the user's request that 'the alt-tab system properly reflect the open windows': the seven-window cap (RECENT_MAX) hid the eighth window and every parked one while the island listed them, and per-step activation would have unparked every parked window walked past, so the cap went and the walk commits on release.

**Consequences.** Revises @legeos.decision.window-groups-are-explicit-and-compositor-owned: Super+Tab no longer cycles groups (subsumed by Taskfield's unit sections, groups first) and Alt+` is the within-unit chord; there is still no Ctrl+Tab. Adds a route to @legeos.decision.the-home-field-is-a-launcher-not-a-search: Super+Space, Enter on a running application activates its most recent window, Ctrl+Enter launches another, the arrow opens Taskfield filtered to it. Fulfils home-taskbar-migration from @legeos.decision.home-projects-and-tool-actions: parked windows are on the island (dimmed) and in Taskfield's shelf band, on Home only when parked into a place. Layer::Presentation (wire 8) sits between SystemModal and ShellOverlay and holds the shell's Taskfield chrome, mapped only inside the mode. templar_shell_manager_v1 v8 adds open_taskfield, taskfield_state and launcher_focus; the Wayland XML is now gated by xtask check-wayland-versions. The window overview is named 'Windows' to a person; Taskfield is the internal name. Alt+Tab and the island now agree on which windows are open; the compositor's switcher HUD lists them by title (falling back to the application's short name), dims parked rows and scrolls a window of rows around the selection when they do not fit; it draws no icons, because the compositor loads none. Work: @legeos.work.task-system, @legeos.work.alt-tab-and-task-rail-icons-20261004.

## legeos.decision.the-home-field-is-a-launcher-not-a-search

### Revision 1 — The Home search is an application launcher over AppIdentity1: applications only, ranked like a launcher; file search belongs to the Files object and to FSearch

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.the-home-field-is-a-launcher-not-a-search/1` · scope `path "crates/templar-session-core/**"`, `path "crates/templar-types/src/action.rs"`, `path "services/templar-sessiond/**"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/**"` · topic `home-search`

The field at the top of bare Home is the application launcher and answers with applications only; it never asks the file service and never says it is searching files. Its one registry is AppIdentity1 — the same inventory that launches, groups variants and carries updates and shortcuts — so an application originates in exactly one place, and a launcher is a view over that inventory rather than a second scanner of .desktop files. It ranks like a launcher: exact name, then name prefix, then a later word of the name, then a substring, then the name as an abbreviation (the query's letters in order, starting a word, gap-penalised), then keywords, then categories, then the identifier as a last resort; within a tier the application launched most recently comes first, from the shell's own recents list, and a boost never lifts a row across a tier. A row's second line is the .desktop name it is installed under, never the shell's internal id. Typing a letter on bare Home opens the search and goes into it; Enter opens the one highlighted row and Escape empties the field. A path typed into it (/etc, ~/src) is an instruction rather than a result and opens that folder in the file manager. A file search belongs to the Files object, scoped to the location it shows (folders before files, capped per source). Projects are tiles and actions have the context menu and cheat sheet, so neither is a search result. Deep search over everything indexed is the job of a real search tool: fsearch is the default candidate of the exclusive ProviderRole::FileSearch, launched with --search <query> from the Files object's last row and a context-menu verb; templar-filed keeps its index for the scoped in-place search.

Added 2026-09-09 by @legeos.decision.task-system-four-scales-one-model, without adding a second launcher: Super+Space reveals Home with this field focused and armed (launcher_focus over templar_shell_v1 v8), so the keyboard route from a fullscreen window to starting something is Super+Space, type, Enter, and the fullscreen window is not disturbed. A result that is already running shows its count ('Firefox · 8 running', from templar_window::task::units); Enter on it activates the application's most recent window (launcher.activate-recent), Ctrl+Enter launches another instance (launcher.launch-new), and the right arrow or Tab opens Taskfield filtered to that application. The launcher still never switches windows as a list: activating is the one exception, and the list of windows is Taskfield's.

**Context.** The user asked for 'an app search, like the cosmic-launcher app search, or that code can be used wholesale in fact if our app search is limited somehow', while keeping the convention of unifying application origination for updates and shortcuts. Both were read at 2026-09-08. cosmic-launcher is a libcosmic/iced application — a second toolkit and a second window system inside a pixelkit shell. pop-launcher, the ranking behind it, is a JSON-over-stdio daemon with its own desktop-entry plugin: adopting it would put a second application registry beside AppIdentity1. The part worth having is about 45 lines of scoring; the shell's own MatchKind ladder was already finer on everything pop-launcher scores 1.0 and was missing only a typo-tolerant tail and the recency boost.

**Consequences.** Neither cosmic-launcher nor pop-launcher is vendored, forked or run: the ranking is written in shell/templar-shell/src/app_search.rs with no new dependency. The recency boost reads shell/templar-shell/src/recents.rs and nothing else. AppIdentity1 stays the single place an application is known. The running count and the three keys read the same task::units the island reads, so the launcher and the island cannot disagree about what is running.

## legeos.decision.three-ownership-tiers

### Revision 1 — TemplarOS has three ownership tiers — System, Applications and workloads, Work — and each crossing between them is declared, owned and checked

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.three-ownership-tiers/1` · scope `path "cli/templar/**"`, `path "crates/templar-appd/**"`, `path "crates/templar-types/**"`, `path "distro/**"`, `path "docs/architecture/**"`, `path "installer/**"`, `path "services/**"`, `path "session/**"` · topic `ownership-tiers`

Three tiers, each with one owner and one way in.
SYSTEM — the versioned Templar deployment: the root subvolume a deployment boots, with the package database that describes it, kernel, initramfs and boot entry. Owner: templar-hostd. Way in: a hostd transaction that snapshots into @deployments/<id>, runs apt into the candidate, seals it and stages it; boot-health promotes or rolls back. The booted deployment is mounted read-only once that path is complete; until then every route that runs apt against the live root is a named, temporary exception. Persistent machine state (logs, hostd's registry, network and machine configuration that must survive a rollback) lives in @var, and what moves with a deployment versus what persists across deployments is declared path by path.
APPLICATIONS AND WORKLOADS — what runs. Owner: templar-sessiond (appd identity, Launcher1) for identity and launch, templar-resourced for pressure policy. An application's record is the authority from installation through execution: identity, executable, icon, associations, resource class, update owner, sandbox. Applications the owner adds come from Flatpak (@legeos.decision.flatpak-and-crash-handling) or are Templar-built packages that enter through the System tier; an application never writes the deployment. A workload is work an application starts that is not the application (a build from a terminal): it gets its own unit and an identity that names the application that spawned it, so the governor never has to guess.
WORK — the owner's projects, documents and application state: @home and the optional /data role. Owner: the person; filed and Homegarden observe it. No System-tier operation writes it; a system service that reads or snapshots it does so through a declared exception (hostd's index checkpoint of @home is the one today).
UBUNTU AND TEMPLAR — Ubuntu is the upstream source and compatibility base and owns core userspace, libraries, hardware enablement, firmware, kernel and security maintenance (the inherited tier of @legeos.decision.three-package-tiers). Templar owns the session, compositor, shell, application identity, file services, resource policy, the update and recovery path, and the interaction model. apt is a System-tier tool used by hostd on a candidate, not a way for the person or an application to change the running system.

**Context.** The owner asked (2026-10-02) to begin enforcing boundaries between OS levels, after an advisor's reading of Nitrux: take the separation principle (OS as chassis, applications outside it, persistent state separate), not Nitrux's implementation (NX Overlayroot, XFS/F2FS layout, no package manager, OpenRC, Hyprland). Today the tiers exist as subvolumes and services but leak: @legeos.observation.hostd-stages-candidates-outside-the-declared-deployments-subvolume, @legeos.observation.the-system-root-is-mutable-in-place-and-its-package-database-lives-in-var, @legeos.observation.terminal-workloads-inherit-the-terminal-identity. Open for the owner before this leaves proposed: (a) whether the person may still apt-install into the system at all once the deployment is read-only, or only through a hostd transaction (a 'templar install <deb>' that stages a candidate); (b) where dpkg state lives: with the deployment (inside the root subvolume) or in @var with a per-deployment copy; (c) the workload route: a per-command scope from the shell hook, a terminal-integrated launcher, or opt-in only; (d) which everyday applications beyond the browser (already a Flathub ref per ADR-0011, distro/seeds/selection.toml layer browser) leave the System tier for Flatpak, and which stay Templar-shipped packages, decided per application.

**Consequences.** systemd stays (cgroups are what the Applications tier stands on), APT/Debian packaging stays (@legeos.constraint.first-release-scope), Btrfs subvolumes stay as the mechanism. ADR-0004's open 'snapshot deployments vs A/B images' is answered as snapshot deployments under @deployments. templar dev deploy, the provisioner's chroot and scripts/update-templaros.sh each become either a hostd transaction or a declared exception. resourced's discovery widens beyond app-templaros-* units to workload and Flatpak scopes.

## legeos.decision.three-package-tiers

### Revision 1 — Every package on a LegeOS medium is native, rebuilt or inherited, and a rebuild needs a stated reason

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.three-package-tiers/1` · scope `path "distro/**"`, `path "tools/xtask/src/seeds.rs"` · topic `package-tiers`

LegeOS is a source-integrated Ubuntu derivative with three package tiers. Native: built by this repository (the workspace packages, the metapackages, the pinned forks). Rebuilt: Ubuntu source plus a LegeOS patch queue, versioned with a +legeos<n> suffix, entered only with a recorded one-line answer to "what changes because LegeOS builds this?" — the tier is empty today on purpose. Inherited: Ubuntu 26.04 binaries as they are, which is everything else, including the kernel, the NVIDIA LRM and CUDA for this edition so Secure Boot works with Canonical's chain and no LegeOS key. The closure report tags every direct package with its tier and asks apt only about inherited names; the medium carries a TIERS.manifest naming the tier of every installed package.

**Context.** Outside advice compared a pure binary derivative with a full source rebuild and recommended the middle: own composition first, a cheap rebuild pipeline second, rebuilds only where a patch, trim or optimisation is measured. The first closure against resolute found three names that needed changing and sixteen native names that had been making the simulation empty.

**Consequences.** No Ubuntu Desktop underneath: composition is the seeds. The rebuild pipeline (source import, build in a clean chroot, publish) is built after LegeOS self-hosts, not before, and its first exercise is a zero-patch rebuild to prove the shape. Moving a package to Rebuilt is a ledger event, not a build detail.

## legeos.decision.toolchain-licence-namespace

### Revision 4 — D8/ADR-0008 — Rust 2024 edition, dev toolchain 1.97.1, MSRV 1.97, AGPL-3.0 own code, org.legeos namespace

`active` · `@legeos.decision.toolchain-licence-namespace/4` · scope `path "Cargo.toml"`, `path "LICENSE"`, `path "crates/templar-types/src/dbus.rs"`, `path "deny.toml"`, `path "rust-toolchain.toml"`

Edition 2024, resolver 3; rust-toolchain.toml pins 1.97.1 for development; workspace rust-version = "1.97" with an MSRV CI job. Rust 1.97 is the honest floor of the resolved workspace because the first-party preview dependency graph already requires it; LegeOS does not claim a lower archive baseline that Cargo cannot resolve. Own code is AGPL-3.0-only (repository-wide LICENSE), with lege-comp retaining its GPL-3.0-only exception; forks keep upstream licences; deny.toml holds the licence allow-list; DEP-5 debian/copyright is regenerated by cargo xtask copyright. Reverse-DNS namespace org.legeos for D-Bus names, app IDs and first-party apps (org.legeos.Session/.Resources/.Files/.Host; org.legeos.Files, org.legeos.Viewer); polkit org.legeos.host.*; env LEGEOS_APP_ID / LEGEOS_INSTANCE_ID.

**Context.** The planning workspace used edition 2024 + MPL-2.0 and org.example placeholders; the archive build must work with the distribution's own rustc.

**Consequences.** One namespace everywhere; archive-buildable without a newer toolchain.

## legeos.decision.window-groups-are-explicit-and-compositor-owned

### Revision 1 — Window groups are explicit, owned by templar-window, stacked as one, placed beside on grouping, outlined as one, and one chip on the island; Alt+Tab across every window, Alt+` within the unit, Super+Tab opens Taskfield

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.window-groups-are-explicit-and-compositor-owned/1` · scope `path "compositor/templar-comp/**"`, `path "crates/templar-field/**"`, `path "crates/templar-window/**"`, `path "interfaces/wayland/**"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/**"` · topic `window-groups`

A window group is an explicit, user-made set of two or more application windows that behave as one unit of work. Seven rules: (1) groups are explicit — made by dropping one window's title band on another's band, or by the Super+G chord; never inferred from proximity, application or time. (2) The compositor owns groups through WindowService: membership lives in templar-window, the shell learns it over templar_shell_v1 (toplevel v3 `group` event), so every switcher works with the shell dead. (3) A group is one thing to stack: activating any member raises every member contiguously, relative order kept, the activated one on top; geometry never changes. (4) Chords, revised 2026-09-09 by @legeos.decision.task-system-four-scales-one-model: Alt+Tab / Alt+Shift+Tab walk the seven most recently activated windows across every unit and output, never scoped to a group (the original scoping, withdrawn 2026-09-08, made a group a place Alt+Tab could not leave). Alt+` / Alt+Shift+` walk the current task unit — the group's members when the focused window is grouped, the application's windows otherwise — so the group feature still costs nothing until a group exists. Super+Tab opens Taskfield, whose sections are task units with explicit groups first, so 'across groups' is subsumed rather than lost; there is no separate group-cycle chord any more. Both switchers walk a list frozen at the first press and released with the modifier (templar_window::SwitchRing), because every step activates and activation raises. (5) A group has at least two members; it dissolves when the second-to-last leaves or closes, and its chip goes with it. (6) Grouping places, it never merges: the dropped or chorded window is set down beside the target on the nearest free side, edge to edge; nothing is stacked, tabbed or folded into one frame; only the band is a drop target; a band drag moves the whole group and Shift+drag moves one member; in Taskfield, dropping a card on another section groups the same way. (7) A group is visibly one thing: a two-pixel outline in the group's accent around the union of the members' rectangles, the same colour as a stripe in each member's band, its island chip and its Taskfield section; the accent is assigned from a short palette by group id in templar-window. Super+G groups with the previously focused window; Super+Shift+G ungroups. There is no Ctrl+Tab binding and no setting for any of this. A group appears once on the island, keyed `group:<id>` — never on Home.

**Context.** The user asked on 2026-09-03 for grouped windows that can be dragged together as one window group, with Alt+Tab switching inside a group and Ctrl+Tab between groups. On reading the plan the user chose Super+Tab outright (Ctrl+Tab belongs to tabbed applications), and specified that dropping one window on another must place it beside the other rather than combine them, with a coloured outline around the whole group as the indicator. Revised 2026-09-08: the Home half was withdrawn — a running window, and so a group, is work in progress and lives on the bar and nowhere else. Revised 2026-09-09: the Task System decision gives Super+Tab to Taskfield. Cycling groups by their last-active member was one linear list too many; Taskfield's top level already shows every unit with groups first, and the within-unit walk that a group needs is Alt+`. WindowService::group_cycle_targets and the window.group-cycle-* actions are deleted; window.within-unit-forward/backward take their place with the fan as the pointer route.

**Consequences.** Plan in docs/planning/window-groups-and-application-integration.md §2–3 and @legeos.work.window-groups (WG1 model, WG2 compositor, WG3 protocol, WG5 hands-on); the chord swap and the Taskfield drop-to-group are in @legeos.work.task-system. The existing Super+Left/Right spatial step keeps its stored-nothing semantics as window.step-right/left. Applications keep Ctrl+Tab. The group accent palette becomes per-theme when the two themes land (@legeos.decision.appearance-is-a-working-field-with-two-themes). From the 2026-09-08 revision: WG4's Home tile is superseded by the island chip (`taskbar::Entry::key` is `group:<id>`); the fan is the successor consumer of the parked and group tiles' drawing.

## legeos.decision.window-tabs-are-external-revealed-and-stationary

### Revision 1 — A window's tabs live outside it on one chosen side, appear when the pointer asks, never resize the client and never move during an interaction

`proposed` · `@legeos.decision.window-tabs-are-external-revealed-and-stationary/1` · scope `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/chrome/**"`, `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/input.rs"`, `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/space_sync.rs"`, `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/xdg_shell.rs"`, `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/xwayland.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-session-core/src/settings.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-window/**"`, `path "interfaces/wayland/templar-shell-v1.xml"` · topic `window-tabs`

Application pixels belong to the application; a window's name tag and its controls (Park, Maximize, Close) belong to the compositor and live outside the client, on one side of it. Five rules.
(1) One side per window, from TabSide {Top, Bottom, Left, Right}. The default comes from a setting (windows.tabs.side, default top: the owner's hand reaches for the top). A window's side changes only by an explicit act (a per-window choice from the name tag) or, when windows.tabs.follow-resize is on, from the latched edge of a resize grab, applied after the grab ends. Never from instantaneous pointer direction.
(2) Stationary: the tabs have a fixed anchor on their side. They never follow the pointer, and while one is pressed or a drag/resize grab runs, side and visibility are latched until the grab ends.
(3) Revealed, not permanent (windows.tabs.reveal = hover by default, always as the discoverable fallback). Hidden tabs take no input: the exterior band where they would appear belongs to whatever is under it until the pointer rests there and the tabs are drawn. A reveal never activates anything; Close needs its own click on a visible Close. Leaving has a short grace. A window's hidden tabs never take input from a window stacked above it at that point.
(4) Tabs never reconfigure the client. The client rectangle is the window's geometry; showing, hiding or changing side of the tabs sends no configure and changes no client size. One authoritative layout from WindowService (client, side, name and control rectangles, reveal band, resize zones, recovery target) is what chrome drawing, press routing, dwell, recovery and damage all read.
(5) Resize owns the corners. The exterior corner squares of every window are resize zones whatever side its tabs are on, and the tabs are inset from them, so Close and resize never compete for one press location.
Where there is no exterior room on the chosen side (a window flush with the output edge, maximized, fullscreen) the tabs are drawn over the client's own edge on a dwell, as covering_chrome does for a screen-filling window today; that is an overlay and is named as one, not external.

**Context.** Today the tags are a permanent 32 px strip fixed to the bottom of the frame and subtracted from the client (geometry::client_area, tag_strip), Close sits under the client's visible bottom-right corner (@legeos.observation.close-tag-sits-under-the-client-bottom-right-corner), and the owner wants tabs that can appear on any side, possibly chosen by resizing, possibly revealed on mouseover. The 2026-10-01 advisor recommended stationary anchors with exterior hover reveal as the default, resize-chosen placement only as a latched, post-grab hint, and exhausting top/bottom before vertical sides. Open for the owner before this leaves proposed: (a) default side top versus bottom; (b) reveal trigger, a dwell in the exterior band versus immediate entry; (c) a discoverability gesture that shows every tab and resize zone at once (bare Super is taken by Home reveal); (d) how Left/Right sides arrange a horizontal name tag (rotated text is ruled out).

**Consequences.** geometry::client_area, frame_around and tag_strip as the frame/strip relationship are removed in a clean cutover; MIN_WINDOW_HEIGHT and the recovery rules are restated against the tab side. A window gains 32 px of client height at the same geometry. is_recoverable/repair_window guarantee a reachable tab anchor on the chosen side or the overlay fallback. The bottom-centre gesture gate and the bottom-edge peek keep priority over a bottom-side reveal band at the output's bottom edge. Amends the tags half of @legeos.decision.one-persistent-bottom-bar-tags-not-bands (tags stay, the bottom strip goes).
